title: Part 1, Chapter 12
paragraphs: What a goatherd told the company with Don Quixote
Just then another young man arrived, one of those who carried provisions up from the village, and he said, "Do you know what's happening in the village, friends?"
"How would we know?" one of them replied.

"Well, listen to this," the young man went on. "This morning that famous student-shepherd named Chrysostom died, and the rumor is that he died of love for that devil of a village girl, the daughter of Guillermo the Rich — the one who roams the open country around here dressed as a shepherdess."
"You mean Marcela?" said one of them.

"That's the one," the goatherd answered. "And here's the strangest part: he stated in his will that he wants to be buried out in the fields, like a Moor, at the foot of the rock by the Cork-tree spring, because — so the story goes, and they say he said it himself — that was the spot where he first laid eyes on her. He left other instructions too, which the village clergy say should not and must not be carried out, because they smack of paganism. But his great friend Ambrosio, the student who dressed as a shepherd alongside him, insists that everything must be done exactly as Chrysostom directed, with nothing left out, and the whole village is in an uproar over it. Still, word is that in the end Ambrosio and his shepherd friends will get their way, and tomorrow they're coming to bury him with great ceremony in the place I mentioned. I'm sure it will be something worth seeing; at any rate, I won't miss it, even if I knew I couldn't get back to the village tomorrow."
"We'll all do the same," the goatherds answered, "and we'll draw lots to see who has to stay behind and watch everyone's goats."

"Good thinking, Pedro," said one, "though there's no need to go to that trouble — I'll stay behind for all of you. And don't put it down to virtue or a lack of curiosity on my part; it's just that the splinter that went into my foot the other day won't let me walk."
"We thank you all the same," Pedro answered.

Don Quixote asked Pedro to tell him who the dead man was and who the shepherdess was. Pedro replied that all he knew was that the dead man had been a wealthy gentleman from a village in those mountains who had studied at Salamanca for many years and then come home with a reputation for being very learned and widely read. "Above all, people said, he was an expert in the science of the stars and everything that goes on up there in the sky with the sun and the moon — he used to tell us the cris of the sun and moon down to the exact moment."

"It's called an eclipse, my friend, not a cris — the darkening of those two great lights," said Don Quixote. But Pedro, not bothering with such trifles, carried on with his story: "He also predicted when a year was going to bring abundance or estility."
"Sterility, you mean," said Don Quixote.

"Sterility or estility," Pedro answered, "it comes to the same thing in the end. And I can tell you that his father and the friends who trusted him got very rich by following his advice, because he would tell them: 'Sow barley this year, not wheat; this year you can plant beans but not barley; next year there'll be a bumper olive crop, and for the three years after that you won't get a drop of oil.'"
"That science is called astrology," said Don Quixote.

"I don't know what it's called," Pedro replied, "but I do know he knew all that and more besides. Anyway, to cut it short: not many months after he came back from Salamanca, he showed up one day dressed as a shepherd, with a crook and a sheepskin, having thrown off the long gown he'd worn as a scholar; and at the same time his great friend Ambrosio, who had been his companion in his studies, put on shepherd's clothes along with him. I forgot to mention that Chrysostom, the one who's dead, was a great hand at writing verses — so much so that he wrote the carols for Christmas Eve and the plays for Corpus Christi that the young men of our village performed, and everyone said they were excellent. When the villagers saw the two scholars suddenly appear in shepherd's dress, they were astonished and couldn't guess what had driven them to such a bizarre change. Around this time our Chrysostom's father died, and he inherited a great deal of property, in goods as well as land, no small number of cattle and sheep, and a large sum of money. The young man was left absolute master of all of it, and honestly, he deserved every bit, because he was a very good companion, kind-hearted, a friend to decent people, and with a face like a blessing. Before long it came out that he had changed his clothes for no other reason than to wander these wild places chasing after that shepherdess Marcela our lad mentioned a moment ago, because the late Chrysostom had fallen in love with her. And now I must tell you — because you ought to know — who this girl is. Perhaps, or rather without any perhaps, you'll never have heard anything like it in all the days of your life, even if you live more years than sarna."
"Say Sarra," said Don Quixote, unable to bear the goatherd's mangling of words.
"The sarna lives long enough," Pedro answered, "and if you're going to pick at my words at every step, señor, we won't be finished within a year."

"Forgive me, friend," said Don Quixote. "I only mentioned it because there's such a difference between sarna and Sarra. But you've answered very well, since the sarna does outlive Sarra — so go on with your story, and I won't object to anything else."

"Well then, my dear sir," said the goatherd, "in our village there was a farmer even richer than Chrysostom's father, named Guillermo, and God gave him, on top of his great wealth, a daughter whose mother died giving birth to her — and she was the most respected woman in this whole district. I can picture her even now, with that face that seemed to carry the sun on one side and the moon on the other; and on top of that she was hardworking and kind to the poor, which is why I trust her soul is at this very moment in bliss with God in the next world. Her husband Guillermo died of grief at losing such a good wife, leaving his daughter Marcela, a child and an heiress, in the care of one of her uncles, a priest who held a benefice in our village. The girl grew up so beautiful that she reminded us of her mother, whose beauty was remarkable — and yet people thought the daughter's would surpass it. And so it was that when she reached fourteen or fifteen, nobody could look at her without blessing God for making her so beautiful, and most of them fell hopelessly in love with her. Her uncle kept her closely sheltered and out of sight, but even so, the fame of her great beauty spread until, both for that and for her great fortune, her uncle was asked, pressed, and pestered to give her in marriage — not only by men from our town but by men from many leagues around, including some of the highest standing among them. But being a good Christian, although he wanted to marry her off promptly once he saw she was of age, he refused to do it without her consent — and not because he had any eye on the income and profit her property brought him while he kept putting off her marriage. And believe me, this was said in praise of the good priest in more than one circle in town. Because I'd have you know, Sir Errant, that in these little villages everything gets talked about and everything gets criticized, and you can be as sure as I am that a priest has to be exceptionally good before he can force his parishioners to speak well of him — especially in villages."
"That's the truth," said Don Quixote, "but go on, for the story is very good, and you, good Pedro, tell it with real style."

"May the Lord's grace never fail me," said Pedro, "that's the style that matters. To continue: you should know that although the uncle laid out for his niece the qualities of each one of her many suitors in particular, urging her to marry and choose whichever suited her own taste, she never gave any answer except that she had no wish to marry yet, and that being so young, she didn't feel ready to carry the burden of married life. Faced with these apparently reasonable excuses, her uncle stopped pressing her and decided to wait until she was a bit older and could choose a partner to her own liking. Because, he said — and he was quite right — parents shouldn't force their children into a settled life against their will. But then, when no one expected it, what do you know — one day the demure Marcela appears, transformed into a shepherdess; and despite her uncle and everyone in town who tried to talk her out of it, she took to going out into the fields with the other shepherd girls of the village and tending her own flock. And from the moment she appeared in public and her beauty could be seen in the open, I honestly couldn't tell you how many rich young men, gentlemen and farmers alike, have put on Chrysostom's kind of costume and gone roaming these fields courting her. One of them, as I've already said, was our dead friend, who people say didn't just love her but worshipped her. But don't imagine, just because Marcela chose a life of such freedom and independence, with little privacy or rather none at all, that she has given the slightest occasion — or even the appearance of one — to cast doubt on her purity and modesty. On the contrary, she guards her honor with such vigilance, and so much of it, that of all the men who court and pursue her, not one has boasted, or could truthfully boast, that she ever gave him the smallest hope of getting what he wanted. For although she doesn't avoid or shun the company and conversation of the shepherds, and treats them with courtesy and kindness, the moment any one of them comes to declare his intentions — even intentions as proper and holy as marriage — she hurls him away from her like a catapult. And with this temperament of hers she does more damage in this country than if the plague had broken out in it, because her friendliness and her beauty draw the hearts of those around her into loving and courting her, while her scorn and her plain speaking drive them to the edge of despair; so they don't know what to say except to call her out loud cruel and hard-hearted, and other names of that sort that describe her character well enough. And if you stayed here any length of time, señor, you would hear these hills and valleys echoing with the laments of the rejected men who chase after her. Not far from here there's a spot with a couple of dozen tall beech trees, and there isn't one of them that doesn't have the name of Marcela carved and written into its smooth bark — and above some of them a crown carved into the same tree, as if her admirer wanted to say more plainly still that Marcela wears and deserves the crown of all human beauty. Here one shepherd sighs, there another grieves; over there you hear love songs, over here despairing laments. One of them will spend all the hours of the night sitting at the foot of some oak or rock, and the sun finds him there in the morning, his weeping eyes never having closed, dazed and out of his senses; another, giving his sighs no rest or relief, lies stretched on the burning sand in the full heat of the sweltering summer noon, sending up his appeal to the merciful heavens — and over this one and that one, over these and all of them, the beautiful Marcela triumphs, free and unconcerned. All of us who know her are waiting to see where her pride will end, and who the lucky man will be who manages to tame so formidable a nature and take possession of a beauty so supreme. Since everything I've told you is well-established fact, I'm convinced that what they say about the cause of Chrysostom's death, the way our lad told it, is the truth as well. So I advise you, señor, don't fail to be at his burial tomorrow. It will be well worth watching, because Chrysostom had many friends, and the place where he asked to be buried isn't half a league from here."
"I'll make a point of it," said Don Quixote, "and I thank you for the pleasure you've given me by telling such a fascinating story."

"Oh," said the goatherd, "I don't know even half of what has happened to Marcela's lovers, but perhaps tomorrow we'll run into some shepherd on the road who can tell us. For now you'd do well to go and sleep under a roof, because the night air could harm your wound — though with the remedy I've put on it, there's no fear of any complication."

Sancho Panza, who was wishing the goatherd's endless talking to the devil, urged his master for his part to come and sleep in Pedro's hut. He did so, and spent the whole rest of the night thinking about his lady Dulcinea, in imitation of Marcela's lovers. Sancho Panza settled himself down between Rocinante and his donkey and slept — not like a rejected lover, but like a man who had been thoroughly kicked.
